```{r setup, include=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>",
                     fig.width = 9, fig.height = 8)
```

Build a prefecture map with three choices in its dropdown, then try different
legends, a regional inset, and static figures. This tutorial uses bundled
population data and geographic boundaries, so it runs without downloading
data. It requires offlineatlas 0.0.14 or later.

The three choices are **population in 2020**, **preliminary population in
2025**, and **population change from 2020 to 2025**. These are separate
variables on one map, not a playback timeline. Change is a number of people,
not a percentage or an annual growth rate.

## 1. Read the population table

```{r population-data}
library(offlineatlas)
stopifnot(packageVersion("offlineatlas") >= "0.0.14")

# Read the installed CSV. No working-directory adjustment is needed.
population <- example_data("japan_prefecture_population_2020_2025")
head(population)
names(population)

# There should be one row per prefecture and no duplicate keys.
stopifnot(
  nrow(population) == 47,
  !anyDuplicated(population$prefecture_id),
  !anyNA(population$population_2020),
  !anyNA(population$population_2025)
)

# Recalculate the change to show exactly what it means.
# Negative values mean fewer residents in 2025 than in 2020.
population$population_change <-
  population$population_2025 - population$population_2020

colSums(population[c("population_2020", "population_2025", "population_change")])
```

The counts describe October 1 of each year. They were transcribed from a
fixed Wikipedia revision, with normalized English names and a derived join
key. The source identifies the 2025 figures as **preliminary census counts**.
They have not been independently reconciled to the official e-Stat table.
The totals match the national totals in the source snapshot, which checks
the transcription rather than independently validating the source.

The extra `population_change_pct` column contains percentage change, but is
not used in this map. For example, `1.41` in that column means 1.41%, not 141%.
The figures are counts, so inflation adjustment does not apply.

```{r population-notice, eval=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
file.show(example_file("JAPAN-NOTICE.txt"))
```

## 2. Read and inspect the prefecture boundaries

```{r prefecture-boundaries}
# Read all 47 prefectures as an sf object.
prefectures <- sf::st_read(
  example_file("japan_prefectures_sf.geojson"),
  quiet = TRUE
)

head(sf::st_drop_geometry(prefectures))
sf::st_crs(prefectures)
sf::st_bbox(prefectures)

stopifnot(
  nrow(prefectures) == 47,
  !anyDuplicated(prefectures$prefecture_id),
  all(sf::st_is_valid(prefectures))
)
```

These are simplified geoBoundaries prefecture shapes derived from
OpenStreetMap/Wambacher, representing 2017. They are used as a fixed display
snapshot for both population years, not as a reconstruction of boundaries
at each census. The supplied islands remain in the file. Tokyo's remote
islands extend the full map well east of the main archipelago.

`prefecture_id` is a lowercase English key prepared for these two bundled
files. It is not an official Japanese code. The boundary table also retains
the provider's `shapeISO` field. Do not assume another source uses the same
names or identifiers.

## 3. Join the observations to the shapes

```{r join-population}
# Both differences should be character(0), meaning no unmatched keys.
setdiff(population$prefecture_id, prefectures$prefecture_id)
setdiff(prefectures$prefecture_id, population$prefecture_id)
stopifnot(setequal(population$prefecture_id, prefectures$prefecture_id))

# Keep the label already present in the boundary table.
# Only attach the columns needed for this map.
values <- population[c(
  "prefecture_id", "population_2020", "population_2025", "population_change"
)]
japan_data <- merge(
  prefectures, values,
  by = "prefecture_id", all.x = TRUE
)

stopifnot(
  nrow(japan_data) == 47,
  !anyNA(japan_data$population_2020),
  !anyNA(japan_data$population_2025),
  !anyNA(japan_data$population_change)
)
```

Checking the join matters even when the map appears to draw correctly.
An unmatched area must not silently become a zero-population prefecture.

## 4. Start with one year

```{r first-japan-map}
# Use a temporary folder while learning. Replace it with "japan_maps"
# or another folder you own if you want to keep the exported files.
output_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "offlineatlas-japan")
dir.create(output_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

# Five thresholds define six color intervals.
# Reuse these for both years so identical colors mean identical ranges.
population_breaks <- c(1000000, 2000000, 4000000, 6000000, 10000000)

japan_base <- atlas(
  title = "Population across Japan's prefectures",
  units = "people",
  entity_name = "prefecture",
  entity_names = "prefectures",
  notice = paste(
    "October 1 counts; 2025 figures are preliminary.",
    "Change is 2025 minus 2020. Fixed 2017 display boundaries.",
    "Source snapshot has not been independently reconciled to the official table."
  ),
  sources = c(
    paste(
      "Population: Wikipedia contributors, List of Japanese prefectures by population,",
      "revision 1384069728, CC BY-SA 4.0; names normalized and change recalculated.",
      "https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Japanese_prefectures_by_population&oldid=1384069728",
      "https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/"
    ),
    paste(
      "Boundaries: copyright OpenStreetMap contributors, via Wambacher / geoBoundaries,",
      "JPN ADM1, 2017; simplified geometry, labels normalized and coordinates rounded.",
      "Adapted database under ODbL 1.0; retain attribution and license notices.",
      "https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright",
      "https://opendatacommons.org/licenses/odbl/1-0/",
      "Machine-readable adapted boundaries are bundled as japan_prefectures_sf.geojson."
    )
  )
)

japan_2020 <- add_areas(
  japan_base,
  data = japan_data,
  id = "prefecture_id",
  label = "prefecture",
  values = "population_2020",
  labels = "Population in 2020",
  breaks = list(population_breaks)
)

# With sf input, omit bounds to fit every supplied feature.
japan_2020 <- set_view(japan_2020, title = "Japan and its supplied islands")

export_html(
  japan_2020,
  file.path(output_dir, "japan-population-2020.html"),
  compress = TRUE, overwrite = TRUE
)
```

## 5. Add the three-choice dropdown

```{r japan-dropdown}
# Begin with the empty base again because add_areas() adds one area layer.
# Do not call add_areas() on japan_2020, which already has that layer.
japan_map <- add_areas(
  japan_base,
  data = japan_data,
  id = "prefecture_id",
  label = "prefecture",
  values = c("population_2020", "population_2025", "population_change"),
  labels = c(
    "Population in 2020",
    "Population in 2025 (preliminary)",
    "Population change, 2020 to 2025"
  ),
  breaks = list(
    population_breaks,
    population_breaks,
    c(-100000, -50000, 0, 50000, 100000)
  )
)
japan_map <- set_view(japan_map, title = "Japan and its supplied islands")

summary(japan_map)

export_html(
  japan_map,
  file.path(output_dir, "japan-population-dropdown.html"),
  compress = TRUE, overwrite = TRUE
)
```

The order of `values`, `labels`, and `breaks` must agree. A value exactly on
a threshold enters the higher interval. The two population years use the
same thresholds; change uses its own negative and positive thresholds.

## 6. Give population and change different palettes

```{r japan-palettes}
blues <- c("#6BAED6", "#4292C6", "#2171B5", "#08519C", "#083E7D", "#062B58")

# Target both population counts, leaving the change variable separate.
japan_styled <- set_palette(
  japan_map,
  variable = c("population_2020", "population_2025"),
  colors = blues
)

# Warm colors show decline; blue colors show growth.
# Zero has its own neutral key, outside these six intervals.
japan_styled <- set_palette(
  japan_styled,
  variable = "population_change",
  colors = c("#B2182B", "#EF8A62", "#FDDBC7", "#D1E5F0", "#67A9CF", "#2166AC"),
  zero_color = "#E6E6E6",
  zero_label = "No population change"
)

# Apply missing-value and boundary styling to all numeric variables.
# Omitting colors preserves the palettes just assigned.
japan_styled <- set_palette(
  japan_styled,
  missing_color = "#FFFFFF",
  border_color = "#333333",
  border_width = 0.5
)

# These are counts of people, so show whole numbers without a currency sign.
japan_styled <- set_number_format(japan_styled, style = "number", digits = 0)

japan_styled <- set_legend(
  japan_styled, type = "bar", title = "People"
)
japan_styled <- set_selection_card(japan_styled, position = "top_left")

# Rename the dropdown control for this example.
japan_styled <- set_controls(
  japan_styled, labels = c(variable = "Population measure")
)

# Leaving subtitle at NULL uses the active variable in image-download headings.
japan_styled <- set_export_options(
  japan_styled,
  title = "Population across Japan's prefectures",
  prompt = TRUE
)

export_html(
  japan_styled,
  file.path(output_dir, "japan-population.html"),
  compress = TRUE, overwrite = TRUE
)

if (interactive()) {
  browseURL(normalizePath(file.path(output_dir, "japan-population.html")))
}
```

The bar joins equal-width bands for the existing intervals. It is not a
continuous gradient or a proportional numeric axis. Switch the dropdown
between years and change, then select Tokyo to inspect its active value.
Colors, labels, and the selected-value card update together.

## 7. Try other presentations without rebuilding the data

```{r japan-alternatives}
# Keep the styled atlas and create a box-legend alternative.
japan_boxes <- set_legend(
  japan_styled, type = "boxes", title = "People", columns = 3
)
export_html(
  japan_boxes,
  file.path(output_dir, "japan-population-boxes.html"),
  compress = TRUE, overwrite = TRUE
)

# Another version concentrates on the main archipelago.
# A separate geographic inset shows Okinawa and nearby islands.
japan_focused <- set_view(
  japan_styled,
  bounds = c(128, 30, 146, 46),
  title = "Main archipelago"
)
japan_focused <- set_inset(
  japan_focused,
  bounds = c(122, 24, 131, 30),
  title = "Southwestern islands"
)
export_html(
  japan_focused,
  file.path(output_dir, "japan-population-inset.html"),
  compress = TRUE, overwrite = TRUE
)
```

The inset uses actual longitude and latitude; islands are not relocated.
Remote eastern islands fall outside these two focused views but remain in
the data. The full-extent `japan_styled` version shows all supplied geometry.
Selection and the variable dropdown are shared between the main map and inset.

## 8. Make a static figure and save a PDF

```{r japan-static}
# Choose a single variable. The full-extent atlas has no inset to omit.
change_figure <- as_ggplot(
  japan_styled, variable = "population_change"
) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    title = "Population change across Japan's prefectures",
    subtitle = "2025 minus 2020, in people; 2025 counts are preliminary",
    caption = paste(
      "Population: Wikipedia contributors (CC BY-SA 4.0), revision 1384069728.",
      "Boundaries: OpenStreetMap contributors / Wambacher / geoBoundaries (ODbL 1.0), 2017.",
      "Fixed display boundaries; source counts not independently reconciled to official data.",
      sep = "\n"
    )
  )
print(change_figure)

dir.create(file.path(output_dir, "static"), showWarnings = FALSE)
ggplot2::ggsave(
  file.path(output_dir, "static", "japan-population-change.pdf"),
  plot = change_figure, width = 10, height = 9, units = "in", bg = "white"
)
ggplot2::ggsave(
  file.path(output_dir, "static", "japan-population-change.png"),
  plot = change_figure, width = 10, height = 9, dpi = 150, bg = "white"
)
```

`as_ggplot()` returns an editable ggplot2 figure. Its `variable` argument
selects what to draw; the browser's current selection is not sent back to R.
Set static headings with `ggplot2::labs()`. Browser selection cards and
download-heading dialogs do not apply to this static figure. Visible browser
insets are also omitted by `as_ggplot()`, with a warning.

## 9. Find other boundaries

The bundled shapes make this tutorial reproducible, but you can use other
`sf` polygons. For Japanese boundaries, possible sources include
[MLIT's administrative-area downloads](https://nlftp.mlit.go.jp/ksj/gml/datalist/KsjTmplt-N03-2025.html)
and [e-Stat's boundary data](https://www.e-stat.go.jp/help/view-on/map/boundary_data).
Check the level, year, format, and reuse terms before downloading.

MLIT N03 files contain municipal features. A download for one prefecture
does not necessarily contain one prefecture polygon. To map prefectures,
combine the municipalities by their prefecture identifier or name first.
For example, after reading an appropriate N03 file into `municipalities`,
inspect `N03_001` and the available administrative codes before grouping.
The Japanese names in the population CSV can help, but still check every match.

```{r alternative-boundaries, eval=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
# Substitute a file you downloaded and inspect it before joining.
other_boundaries <- sf::st_read("path/to/your/boundaries.geojson")
names(other_boundaries)
sf::st_crs(other_boundaries)
sf::st_bbox(other_boundaries)
head(sf::st_drop_geometry(other_boundaries))
```

Use `sf::st_transform()` to convert a known coordinate system. Assigning a
different CRS label with `st_set_crs()` does not transform coordinates.
offlineatlas accepts `sf` input with a known CRS and transforms it for its
fixed browser projection. `set_view()` adjusts the extent, not the projection.
Detailed boundaries increase HTML size, so choose a cartographic or carefully
simplified dataset appropriate to your display scale.

## Sources and sharing

- [Wikipedia's population table, fixed revision](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Japanese_prefectures_by_population&oldid=1384069728),
  adapted under [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/).
- [The official e-Stat table cited by that page](https://www.e-stat.go.jp/en/dbview?sid=0004050397).
- [geoBoundaries Japan ADM1 snapshot](https://github.com/wmgeolab/geoBoundaries/tree/9469f09/releaseData/gbOpen/JPN/ADM1),
  copyright OpenStreetMap contributors, via Wambacher, under
  [ODbL 1.0](https://opendatacommons.org/licenses/odbl/1-0/).

Keep the source notices with redistributed data and figures. The separate
bundled population CSV and adapted GeoJSON provide the machine-readable
snapshots. The package's MIT code license does not replace their data licenses.
The exported HTML embeds data, geometry, scripts, and styles and works offline.
Re-export after changing an R object; existing files do not update themselves.
